text: A refactor that's functionally identical can still quietly add gas cost — an extra storage read, a redundant external call, a less efficient layout. On a contract called thousands of times a day, a silent ten percent gas increase is a real cost regression that none of this chapter's correctness tests would catch, because the contract still behaves correctly — it's just more expensive.

forge snapshot runs your test suite and records every test's gas usage into a dot-gas-snapshot file at the project root. For a fuzz test, the snapshot records the mean and median gas across all runs, not a single number, because gas cost can vary by input even within one function.

Two flags turn that file into an enforceable check. forge snapshot --diff compares current gas usage against the committed snapshot. forge snapshot --check exits with an error if any test now uses more gas than recorded — that's the one that belongs in CI, failing the build the moment a PR silently increases gas cost.

Not every gas increase is a regression — sometimes you're trading gas for a real feature or a necessary safety check. When that's the case, you update the snapshot deliberately: run forge snapshot again, then commit the new dot-gas-snapshot file, which makes the change visible and reviewable in the PR diff instead of a silent creep nobody signed off on.

You're ready for Lesson 6 once you can explain why a contract that passes every fuzz and invariant test would still need a separate gas snapshot check — correctness and cost are two different things to verify.
